title: The Loud Cache
briefing.company: Hamaca sells rooms in small hotels and haciendas across Yucatán, from an office in Mérida. Most guests book from Europe, where it is already morning, and metasearch sites ask for prices all night. Requests come through edge to bookings-api, which reads availability from rooms-cache, queries bookings-db through a pool of connections, and asks channel-mgr, an outside channel manager, for live rates.
briefing.role: You're on call for bookings this week. It's Friday, a few hours before the first flights land in Cancún. The office is dark; Europe is wide awake.
briefing.tonight: 02:58. Availability is slow, and the cache is shouting.
panel.poolUsage: bookings-api → bookings-db · pooled connections by state
panel.poolWait: bookings-api → bookings-db · p99 wait for a connection
runbook.latency.title: bookings-api is slow
runbook.latency.body:
bookings-api answers GET /availability for the site and for metasearch partners. A request looks up availability in rooms-cache, queries bookings-db, and asks channel-mgr for live rates. A slow p99 means one of those waits grew, or a new one appeared.

bookings-db queries also wait for a free connection from the pool before they run. That wait shows in db_client_connections_wait_time_seconds, not in bookings-db's own latency, and a query that waits too long fails without ever reaching the database.

Start with what changed: bookings-api deploys, its pool and cache settings, and other services. Then find the wait that grew.

Restarting bookings-api drops in-flight requests for about a minute and undoes nothing that changed.
runbook.pool.title: bookings-api connection pool
runbook.pool.body:
Each bookings-api instance keeps a pool of up to db.pool.max_size connections to bookings-db, 40 by default. A query borrows a connection and gives it back when the work is done; db_client_connections_use_time_seconds says how long that takes. When every connection is out, the next query waits up to 2 s for one, then fails with "could not acquire connection in 2000 ms".

bookings-db accepts at most 85 connections from bookings-api, split evenly between its instances, and never more than the pool size each. With 2 instances that is 40 each. With 4 it is 21 each: more instances, not more connections.

Leak detection writes a WARN log when a connection has been out for more than 30 s. It is a log line only; nothing alerts on it.

Pool settings live in bookings-api's config and reload without a restart.
runbook.cache.title: rooms-cache (availability cache)
runbook.cache.body:
rooms-cache holds availability per hotel, room type and date. bookings-api decides how long an entry lives (cache.availability.ttl_s, 300 s). A lookup that misses goes to bookings-db instead, so a lower hit ratio means more queries.

Every night at 02:30, rates-sync rewrites availability and rates for every hotel. rooms-cache fills its 6 GB and evicts keys for about two hours: WARN logs, high CPU, and a hit ratio that drops from about 95% to about 80%. It happens every night, and the bookings-db pool is sized for it.

prompt.valeria.ask: Trivo says our availability API keeps timing out and they'll stop showing our hotels for the European morning if it doesn't settle. What's happening, and when is it fixed?
distractor.cacheEviction: The nightly eviction storm made rooms-cache too slow for bookings-api.
distractor.ratesSync: Tonight's rates-sync deploy broke the nightly sync.
distractor.dbSlow: bookings-db got slow under the nightly sync.
chain.exhausted: bookings-api's pool has no free connections; queries wait 2 s and fail
chain.partners: Partners and guests get timeouts instead of rooms
variant.a.factor.ratesInTx: bookings-api 5.8.0 asks channel-mgr for live rates while it still holds its bookings-db connection, so every connection stays out about 95 ms longer.
variant.a.factor.heldFull: Connections held twice as long need twice as many: the pools sit at their 80-connection limit and queries queue for one.
variant.a.factor.trickle: Releases are smoke-tested with 20 requests against one instance, where holding a connection longer costs nothing.
variant.a.chain.trickle: Releases are smoke-tested at a trickle
variant.a.chain.change: 02:44 · 5.8.0 holds the connection while it calls channel-mgr
variant.a.chain.held: Each query holds its connection about twice as long
variant.a.debriefNote: The cache was loud, as it is every night from 02:30, and it had nothing to do with this. bookings-db answered as fast as ever; its connections were busy waiting on channel-mgr. Use time doubled the minute 5.8.0 landed, and the pool sat flat at its limit from then on. Scaling would not have helped: bookings-db accepts 85 connections from bookings-api, however many instances share them.
variant.b.factor.shrunk: A config change at 02:42 cut db.pool.max_size from 40 to 10, so the two instances share 20 connections instead of 80.
variant.b.factor.demand: During the nightly sync bookings-api keeps about 50 connections busy at once; with 20, most queries wait the full 2 s and fail.
variant.b.factor.unchecked: Pool settings reload in production with a schema check only: nothing compares the new size with how many connections are in use.
variant.b.chain.unchecked: Pool settings reload with a schema check only
variant.b.chain.demand: The nightly sync keeps about 50 connections busy
variant.b.debriefNote: "More than we use" was true for most of the day and false at 02:42, twelve minutes into the sync, when bookings-api needed about 50 connections at once. The pool's maximum dropped to a quarter on the dashboard the same minute. Four instances would have shared 40 connections, still short of 50. The fix was the number in the config.
variant.c.factor.leak: bookings-api 5.8.2 returns early for hotels without a rate plan and never gives that request's connection back to the pool.
variant.c.factor.pileUp: A leaked connection stays out until the process restarts: used connections climb every minute until none are left.
variant.c.factor.warnOnly: Leak detection only writes a WARN log, and nothing alerts on it, so the warnings that started at 02:34 reached nobody.
variant.c.chain.warnOnly: Leak warnings go to a log nobody watches
variant.c.chain.change: 02:33 · 5.8.2 keeps the connection when it skips a hotel
variant.c.chain.pileUp: Leaked connections pile up, two or three a minute
variant.c.debriefNote: A restart looks like a fix here: it frees every leaked connection and the alert goes quiet, then the pool fills up again within a quarter of an hour. Used connections climbed steadily from 02:33 and never came down, which is not the shape of the cache's noise, which began at 02:30 and stayed flat. Rolling back 5.8.2 stopped the leak; a restart only resets the count.
variant.d.factor.ttl: A config change at 02:45 lowered the availability TTL from 300 s to 30 s, and the hit ratio fell to about 40%.
variant.d.factor.misses: Every miss is a query to bookings-db: queries per request almost doubled on top of the nightly sync, and the pool could not hold them.
variant.d.factor.unchecked: Cache settings reload with a schema check only; nobody looked at the hit ratio, or at what it costs bookings-db, before or after.
variant.d.chain.unchecked: Cache settings change without a look at the hit ratio
variant.d.chain.misses: Misses become queries: almost twice as many per request
variant.d.debriefNote: This time the loud cache was guilty, but not for the eviction storm it has every night. The 30-second TTL turned hits into misses, and every miss became a query that needed a connection. Queries per request is the number that moved at 02:45; the evictions looked like any other night's.
